title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 318: The Cartography of Silence
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 318 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Cartography of Silence: Maps, Erasure, and Colonial Power

Paragraph 1. Most people look at street maps or phone map apps and think they show the simple truth. We trust that lines on a map match real mountains, coasts, and country borders. However, history professor Dr. Julian Harley says that mapmaking has never been a completely neutral science. In his book, he explains that maps are tools of political power. Instead of just copying the land, maps can change how people see and control a place.

Paragraph 2. Between the 1500s and 1800s, European empires took over lands in the Americas, Africa, and Australia. Before armies or settlers arrived, military mapmakers drew charts of these regions. They often left out local villages, sacred paths, and old local names. By showing busy lands as empty white spaces on paper, mapmakers made it look acceptable for empires to take those lands.

Paragraph 3. Local people understood their land through rivers, forests, and spoken stories. Colonial mapmakers replaced these natural ideas with straight square lines. They cut wild lands into neat rectangular pieces of private property. These neat blocks could easily be written in government books, taxed by leaders, and sold for money in Europe.

Paragraph 4. The effects of old colonial maps still shape our world today. In the 1800s, European diplomats drew borders across Africa and the Middle East using straight lines and rulers inside meeting rooms. Those straight lines cut directly through local ethnic groups and language communities, causing conflicts that still exist today. Dr. Harley reminds us that every map is an argument, and what a map hides can matter even more than what it shows.
